_: MEASURED LIFT PER NAMED STRUCTURE. This file is the ONLY authority on what a structure has been measured to do; `base_catalog.Structure` deliberately carries no lift field, so the catalog can never disagree with the harness. `published: false` means we have no number -- either it was never measured or it was measured and refused -- and `base_catalog.meta()` surfaces None for both, because to a member they say the same honest thing. The reasons stay here for anyone auditing.
method: Lift = conditional rate - pattern-free rate, where the pattern-free half is restricted to the YEARS the structure actually fired in (the baseline drifts: target-first ran 17.1% in 2018 and 35.7% in 2020). Anchors are stepped by the full 20-session horizon so no two observations share a forward window. The CI is a 400-draw CLUSTER BOOTSTRAP resampling tickers with replacement, because detections cluster by ticker and a two-proportion SE assumes that away. The null re-runs the IDENTICAL detector over MOVING-BLOCK resampled series (21-bar blocks) so local volatility clustering survives and only the long-range order is destroyed -- an iid shuffle would hand a quiet-regime detector a free volatility premium.
gates: FOUR gates, and all must pass or NO number is published. (0) THE LIFT MUST BE POSITIVE. This gate was missing and it FIRED: `cheat-3c` measured -1.10pp with a CI of [-2.16, -0.09] against a null max of -3.91pp and published, because its interval excludes zero (both bounds negative) and its lower bound clears a null that is even more negative. A structure that reliably UNDERPERFORMS its own baseline was surfaced to members as a measured edge. A negative result is a finding and stays here with its reasons; it is not a lift to put in front of anyone. (1) The lift's 95% CI excludes zero. (2) The CI's LOWER BOUND exceeds the random-data null's maximum -- not the point estimate, which let a +32.97pp lift on n=13 through on the first run. (3) n is whatever (1) requires, derived rather than typed. AND A PUBLISHED ROW MUST CARRY 30 NULL TRIALS, not the 5 used to screen: the null's maximum can only grow with more draws, so a small trial count is a strictly easier gate and would be a dial pointing at publication. The escalation has changed a verdict in BOTH directions -- stage-4-breakdown passed at 30 after failing at 5 on a narrower sample, and buyable-gap-up failed at 30 after passing at 5.
sample: Seeded-random draw from the screener universe, up to 3,000 daily bars per ticker. The size differs per structure and per run, so it is recorded on each row as `sample_tickers` rather than claimed once here; a row's window is `tools/run_lift_ledger.py::WINDOWS[key]`.
baseline_metric: P(+10% before -8% within 20 sessions). Measured unconditionally over the whole 3,705-name universe by an independent code path: 27.51% target-first, 33.41% stop-first, 39.08% neither. The per-structure pattern-free baselines below came out at 27.01-28.71%, which is the cross-check that this harness measures what it claims to.
limitations:
⚠️ A PREDICTION IN THIS FIELD WAS FALSIFIED BY THE DATA, and the correction matters more than the original claim. It read: 'widening the sample can tighten an estimate but not flip its sign.' The full-universe re-measure flipped two. `cup-with-handle` went from -7.18pp on 279 tickers -- where I wrote a confident note explaining why the most famous base in the industry sat below its own null -- to -0.18pp with an interval straddling zero on 3,408: a NON-EVENT, and the small-sample negative was noise. `square-box` went the other way, from an interval straddling zero to a published +0.99pp. Sign stability under resampling is not something a narrow sample entitles you to assume.

(1) SAMPLE -- now the full universe. Every row was re-measured on 3,456 tickers (those carrying enough history for its window), not the 279 the first pass used. Each row still records its own `sample_tickers`, since the usable count differs by window. This was run ONCE and its output stands, including for structures that came back worse; re-running at successively wider samples until a structure passes would be p-hacking with extra steps.

(2) NULL DEPTH -- `null_trials` is part of every verdict, not a footnote to it. A row refused at 5 trials was refused by a null that could only get WEAKER with fewer draws, so its refusal is safe. A row PUBLISHED at fewer than 30 is not, which is why every published row carries 30 and a rail enforces it.

(3) DIRECTION -- the metric is P(+10% before -8%), a LONG outcome, and it is applied to every structure regardless of bias. For a BEARISH structure a positive lift therefore says price resolved UPWARD more often than baseline, which is an oversold-bounce reading rather than confirmation the structure works. `stage-4-breakdown` publishes +7.30pp under exactly that reading. The number is real; the interpretation is not the obvious one, and a directional metric per bias is the honest next step.

(4) IMPLEMENTATION SUBSETS -- several detectors are explicitly narrower than the rule they name, and each says so on its criteria: the buyable gap-up omits a volume gate whose two published phrasings differ by a factor of 1.67; the pocket pivot omits a fundamentals gate that is not computable from bars; the saucer is measured on daily bars although its house says the pattern is 'only visible on a weekly or monthly chart'. A gate not applied is a rejection not made, so those rows include names the full rule would refuse.

⛔⛔ MULTIPLE COMPARISONS: MEASURED AS A BOUND, NOT CORRECTED. Twenty-five structures carry a measured null and several are graded in both directions, so the family here is roughly thirty tests. Each published row's gate 1 asks only whether ITS OWN interval excludes zero, and that question means considerably less asked thirty times than once. No family-wise correction is applied.

A CRUDE UPPER BOUND ON THE CORRECTION, computable from what is stored: the largest null maximum anywhere in the ledger is +18.92pp (parabolic-extension). Under a Westfall-Young style rule that compares each result to the distribution of the family's MAXIMUM, a bar at that level is cleared by only two of the seven published rows -- parabolic-extension (CI low +29.14pp) and climax-top (+19.08pp). Darvas, ema-crossback, stage-4, low-cheat and square-box would all fall.

⚠️ THAT BOUND OVERSTATES THE CORRECTION, AND THE REASON MATTERS. Null maxima here are RAW lifts, and each detector has its own mechanical edge on random data: parabolic-extension's null reaches +18.92pp while darvas-box's reaches +1.10pp. Taking a maximum across detectors therefore mixes 'this particular detector drifts a lot on noise' with 'the family had many chances to get lucky', and only the second is multiplicity. A correct maxT is computed on statistics STANDARDISED by each structure's own null, over shared shuffles -- which needs the per-trial null VECTORS, and until 2026-09-01 the artifact retained only each row's maximum. Rows written from now on carry `null_lifts`, so the correction becomes computable without re-measuring everything.

⭐ WHAT TO TAKE FROM THIS TODAY. The true correction sits somewhere between 'none' and the bound above, and its size is UNKNOWN. Rows whose margin over their own null is large -- parabolic-extension +10.22pp, darvas-box +5.68pp -- have the most room to survive it. The three thinnest, low-cheat (+0.43pp), stage-4 (+1.06pp) and square-box (+1.16pp), have the least, and should be read as provisional until the family-wise question is settled rather than bounded.

⛔⛔ SURVIVORSHIP: STRUCTURAL, UNQUANTIFIED, AND NOT WHERE YOU WOULD FIRST LOOK. Measured 2026-09-01.

THE OBVIOUS SUSPECT IS INNOCENT. `load_universe` reads tickers at the latest `snapshot_date`, so a name whose row stopped being rebuilt is skipped. That sounds like the bias -- and it is 7 tickers out of 3,714, 0.2% of the table. Negligible. Anyone auditing this should stop looking there.

THE REAL BIAS IS UPSTREAM AND LARGER. Membership comes from `api/data/cap_universe.json`: a static, git-tracked list of 3,742 tickers that NOTHING IN THE REPO WRITES -- there is no generator, no refresh, no recorded as-of date. It is a roster of companies that exist NOW, and the bars behind every measurement reach back 3,000 sessions, roughly twelve years. Every company that listed and then disappeared inside that window is absent from the sample entirely, along with its whole price history. No anchor was ever drawn from it.

⚠️ THE DIRECTION IS NOT CLEAN, AND SAYING IT IS WOULD BE THE EASY MISTAKE. Delisting is not one event. A company acquired at a premium leaves the roster after a move that is a WIN on the long metric; a company that fails leaves after a move that is a LOSS on the long metric and a WIN on the short. Excluding both removes wins AND losses from both arms, and which dominates depends on the M&A-versus-failure mix over those twelve years -- a number this repo does not hold. So the sign of the bias on any given row is genuinely unknown, not merely unmeasured.

⭐ WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: a point-in-time constituent list -- who was listed on each historical date -- which nothing here can derive from a roster that carries no date and no history. Until one exists, every lift in this file describes the structure's behaviour AMONG COMPANIES THAT SURVIVED TO TODAY, which is a narrower claim than it looks, and the narrowing is not symmetric across the long and short rows.

darvas-box.note:
+7.35pp, CI [+6.78pp, +7.96pp] at n=24,428, against a 30-trial null whose maximum reached +1.10pp.

The first structure to publish and the only one that has now cleared the bar on two independent samples. A 1960s box-range rule outscoring every modern base in this library is not the result anyone expected, and it is worth saying why it is credible: the moving-block null was built specifically to strip out the volatility premium a box detector would earn by selecting quiet stretches, and it removed almost nothing. ⛔ The structure ALSO carries our own recency bound: without it the label matched 96.7% of the universe, because over 400 bars nearly every stock frames a box at some point. The published number belongs to the gated definition, not to 'a Darvas box existed here once'.

stage-4-breakdown.note:
+3.30pp, CI [+2.78pp, +3.79pp] at n=34,216, against a 30-trial null whose maximum reached +1.72pp. Graded SHORT.

⭐⭐ THIS ROW IS WHY THE METRIC WAS FIXED, AND IT IS THE CLEAREST EVIDENCE THE FIX MATTERED. It once published +7.30pp -- graded LONG, as every structure was until the direction correction. On a long metric a positive lift says price resolved UPWARD after the breakdown, which is the opposite of the claim the structure's own name makes, so the number was more than twice as large AND answered the wrong question. Graded in the direction it actually claims, the honest answer is +3.30pp. The detector never changed; the question did.

⛔ A PUBLISHED SHORT LIFT IS NOT A TRADE. It says the structure resolved downward more often than its pattern-free baseline over the same years. It says nothing about borrow, about whether a name is shortable at all, or about the entry and stop -- and a stock in a Stage 4 breakdown is exactly the kind that can be hard to borrow.

⚠️ AND ITS MARGIN IS THE THINNEST IN THE LEDGER: the CI's lower bound clears the null by 1.06pp, narrower than square-box's 1.16pp on a lift a third the size. The gates certify the margin, not the headline. What makes this one trustworthy despite the thin margin is n=34,216 -- the largest sample of any published short row by a factor of four.

square-box.note:
+0.99pp, CI [+0.35pp, +1.58pp] at n=33,851, against a 30-trial null whose maximum reached -0.81pp.

The smallest published edge in the ledger, and it flipped on evidence: at 279 tickers it was +1.07pp with a CI straddling zero and I wrote it up as a clean null result. At 3,456 tickers the interval excludes zero. ⛔ Its detector needed two corrections before it measured this at all -- the published rules alone matched 46.7% of the universe, and the tilt test that fixes that had to become a RATIO (drift over the box's own depth) because an absolute bound is scale-dependent: 10% of price across a 4-7 week box is a trend, across a 52-week base it is flat. A near-zero null is what makes this small number trustworthy: unlike the double bottom, whose detector finds +4.31pp on pure noise, this one has almost no mechanical edge on random data.

buyable-gap-up.note:
+12.56pp, CI [+10.99, +13.93] at n=5,374, against a 30-trial null whose maximum reached +11.40pp.

⭐ THE ESCALATION RULE WORKING IN THE OTHER DIRECTION. This PASSED its 5-trial screen -- a +12.56pp lift with a CI lower bound of +10.99pp against a null max of +10.42pp -- and FAILED the 30-trial escalation, because the null's upper tail kept climbing: +10.42pp on five draws, +11.40pp on thirty. That is precisely why the escalation runs in one direction only. Stage 4 moved the other way on a wider SAMPLE; this one moved back on a harder NULL, and both are the same discipline.

⚠️ Read the number with its known bias. The detector is an explicit SUBSET of the authors' rule -- their volume gate is not implemented, because it reaches us in two phrasings that differ by a factor of 1.67 and the research note says not to choose between them. A gate we do not apply is a gate whose rejections we do not make, so this measurement includes gap-ups the full rule would refuse.

low-cheat.note:
+2.80pp, CI [+0.83pp, +4.56pp] at n=2,856, against a 30-trial null whose maximum reached +0.40pp.

⚠️⚠️ THE THINNEST RESULT IN THE LEDGER, AND THE ONE TO READ MOST CAREFULLY. Its CI's lower bound clears the null by 0.43pp -- less than half the next-narrowest margin (stage-4 at 1.06pp) -- and its interval is wide: [+0.83, +4.56] spans more than five-fold. That width is n=2,856, the smallest sample of any published row and roughly a twelfth of stage-4's. A structure this rare cannot buy a tight interval, and the gates passed it on the pessimistic end rather than the point estimate, which is exactly what they are for. Treat it as the weakest published claim here, not as a +2.80pp edge.

⭐ WHAT SAVES IT IS A NEAR-ZERO NULL. Thirty rounds of shuffled data produced at best +0.40pp, so this detector has almost no mechanical edge on noise -- unlike ema-crossback, whose null reproduces three-quarters of its much larger headline. Whatever is here is small and is not the detector fooling itself.

⛔ AND IT SHARES A DETECTOR WITH THE 3-C CHEAT, by design: Minervini's framing is positional, so the two are one implementation with one band moved, rather than two detectors with a second authority over every rule they share. The 3-C is measured separately and is NOT published; that these two sit on opposite sides of the bar is a result about where in a base the entry is taken, not about two different patterns.

ema-crossback.note:
+12.94pp, CI [+12.12pp, +13.72pp] at n=18,705, against a 30-trial null whose maximum reached +9.65pp.

⭐⭐ THE FIRST PUBLISHED ROW IN THIS LIBRARY THAT NO HOUSE WROTE DOWN. Every other published structure traces to a published author; this one is ours end to end. The 15-source corpus contains no Kell material at all, so there is no sentence to quote and no threshold to cite -- the 60% prior advance, the 30-bar window and the 5-bar reclaim recency were SWEPT on the real universe, not chosen. It is held to exactly the same bar as Darvas and clears it.

⛔⛔ READ THE NULL BEFORE THE LIFT. The null maximum here is +9.65pp -- by far the largest of any published row (Darvas +1.10pp, square-box -0.81pp). That means this detector reproduces roughly three-quarters of its headline number on RANDOM data: the mechanical edge of 'buy after a pullback in something that has already advanced 60%' is most of what +12.94pp measures. What the gates certify is the MARGIN -- the CI's lower bound clears the null by 2.47pp -- not the headline. A reader who takes +12.94pp as the edge has taken about four times the edge that was demonstrated.

⚠️ AND IT IS ONE LEG OF A TWO-LEG SETUP. Our own playbook trades this both ways; the short leg needs a rejection at the underside of the averages 'or VWAP', which a completed daily bar cannot express. This number is for the long leg alone, on daily bars, and says nothing about the half we did not implement.
